newsitem.title: ITALY: Rebel would back Italy govt in confidence vote.
newsitem.headline: Rebel would back Italy govt in confidence vote.

text.p: One of two politicians in Italy's ruling centre-left coalition who voted against its mini-budget at commission stage on Friday said he would back the government if a parliamentary confidence vote was called on the package.

Roberto Villetti, member of a small Socialist party, told reporters after the vote: "We don't want to be part of an unstable government therefore if the government has to call a confidence vote on this question, we will vote for it."
The commission in the lower house of parliament voted 25 against and 24 for the proposed 1997 mini-budget.

The measure, which is for 15.5 trillion lire ($9.1 billion) worth of budget deficit cutting measures, must now go to the full lower house assembly where politicians say the government is likely to have to call a confidence to push it through the chamber.
"If in the (government) majority there are forces like Communist Refoundation which are yanking the rope and threatening to break it, we are yanking it too but not to break it," Villetti said.
The government does not have an outright majority in the lower house, where it relies on the uneasy support of the hard-left Communist Refoundation party.
"At this point the government needs to appeal to all the forces in the majority (coalition) because this budget is going to be approved and therefore with a confidence vote," he said.
The other politician who broke ranks in the commission vote was Giuseppe Bicocchi, a member of another minor party in the ruling coalition.
Bicocchi said in a statement later he had voted 'no' to the mini-budget because it was damaging to business.
"We have said from the start we were against the measures in the decree law because it is punitive towards business and because it doesn't affect current spending," he said.
Bicocchi, who is vice chairman of the lower house budget commission, said the government had made no effort to change the measures so he had had no choice but to vote against it.
"We hope the government will have a rethink for the vote in the full assembly," he said.

"Without measures which affect structural spending and in particular pensions, we cannot enter Europe. Our dissent is therefore a strong signal that there needs to be a change in the government's economic policy," he said.
